title: Reversible hypertension associated with complete heart block in a 6-year-old boy
case_prompt:
A previously healthy 6-year-old boy was transferred for evaluation of incidentally discovered hypertension and bradycardia during workup for a 1-week history of abdominal pain, cough, congestion, frontal headache, and decreased appetite. He had received a 2-day course of prednisolone 4 days earlier, which was discontinued when hypertension was noted. There was no use of over-the-counter decongestants. His perinatal course was notable only for transient tachypnea of the newborn. He had undergone multiple corrections for bilateral club feet and reportedly slept more than peers. Review of prior records showed mild hypertension and low heart rate since age 4½ years. Family history included early-onset hypertension in his father (age 29) and premature cardiac deaths on the maternal side; no renal or thyroid disease was reported.

On examination, he was alert and afebrile. Heart rate was 54 beats per minute, blood pressure was 160/91 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Height and weight were at the 8.7th and 14.5th percentiles, respectively. Cardiovascular exam revealed a grade 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with otherwise normal heart sounds. There were scars on both feet; chest, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were normal.

Initial laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and urinalysis. ECG demonstrated complete heart block with atrioventricular dissociation, junctional escape rhythm, and left axis deviation. Echocardiography revealed no structural heart disease, normal ventricular function, and mild left ventricular hypertrophy. Lyme titers were negative. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (3.44 uIU/mL) and free T4 (11.3 µg/dL) were normal. Plasma renin activity was normal. Renal ultrasound and duplex studies showed no abnormalities or stenosis.

An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor was initiated, and the patient was observed without hypotension or other events. He was discharged with diagnoses of likely congenital complete heart block and primary hypertension and scheduled for outpatient cardiology follow-up.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Increased intracranial pressure considered given headache, hypertension, and bradycardia — “His headache resolved without intervention, and his neurological examination was reassuring.”  
2. Hypothyroidism considered as a cause of bradycardia and hypertension — “Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 3.44 uIU/mL and T4 was 11.3 ug/dL excluding hypothyroidism.”  
3. Renal parenchymal or renovascular hypertension considered — “Renal ultrasound was normal as well as his renal duplex that showed no evidence of hemodynamically significant stenosis bilaterally.”  
4. Lyme carditis considered as a reversible cause of heart block — “Lyme titers were within normal limits.”  
5. Sympathomimetic medication exposure considered for reflex bradycardia from hypertension — “His family denies the use of over-the-counter decongestant medications.”  
6. Congenital structural heart disease (e.g., coarctation) considered for secondary hypertension — “Echocardiography was negative for congenital heart disease and demonstrated normal ventricular function.”
